title: The US Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent paints America as an irritable god and demands allies submit like Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through the op-ed: the louder the threat, the more it proves the US has no means of delivery, and allies have already begun to fend for themselves.
why: It offers a contrarian reading of a seemingly tough Treasury op-ed: theological intimidation mostly doesn't get cashed out, and understanding this lets you predict allies' real hand in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers doing cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risk, and policy researchers trying to judge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription prompts; start directly with the Carney speech and the Bessent op-ed.

points.h: The Treasury Secretary writes America as an angry god
points.body: In his "economic D-Day" op-ed in the Financial Times, Bessent packages the choice facing allies as Pascal's wager. Farrell's dissection: he is effectively saying you must treat America as God, court this irritable deity by every means, or it will strike you with lightning. Farrell likens it to a 17th-century Puritan sermon that could be retitled "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" — except the sinners are the rest of the world. The problem is that this kind of sermon-style intimidation is usually the reaction of a preacher who senses the congregation is leaving, not a sign of strength.

points.h: The louder the shout, the softer the stick
points.body: Roosevelt's line was "speak softly and carry a big stick." Farrell says Bessent's route is the reverse: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China: China is currently the country most capable of supporting Iran, and Bessent simply does not want to answer whether the US would dare bring its wrath down on China if China keeps buying Iranian oil. Farrell thinks markets and governments are all betting it won't. So the op-ed reads more like an empty threat: the more completely it is stated, the more it looks like the US bluffing at an empty table.

points.h: Flexible realism amounts to having no strategy
points.body: Explaining White House behavior with "flexible realism" is throwing a cloth over chaos. Farrell says that once you unpack the phrase, it amounts to one sentence: America does whatever it wants, and other countries had better adjust themselves to fit. What actually makes the White House run is not strategy but the contest for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone orbit around him — except Trump does "a stupid version": as long as he can be the center of everyone's attention, he can make decisions that are extremely stupid in both the long and short term. Other countries' response therefore becomes damage limitation rather than continuing to place bets.

Federalist No. 10's answer was "ambition must be made to counteract ambition": let each person's drive for power cancel out the others', grinding out an equilibrium close to the public interest. Farrell says this mechanism has been dismantled from both ends. One end is the Republican Party: internal dissent has almost vanished, senators who object dare not block openly, and one-party control of all three branches short-circuits the old checks. The other end is the federal agencies: the Supreme Court embraces the "unitary executive" theory, inspectors general are fired or intimidated, and ordinary civil servants are converted into at-will employees who can be dismissed at any time. With a person at the top of the system who is utterly unqualified, mistakes get amplified into nationwide madness.

points.h: Rebuilding American institutions starts with learning to experiment
points.body: Farrell does not think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he also does not think America is doomed to slide into disaster. The sample he likes is the experiment New York Mayor Mamdani is running: build a feedback loop between city government and the public, turn people's real troubles into policy, and use social media to let the public see "I'm listening, and I'm doing." He deliberately links this style to Roosevelt's "bold, persistent experimentation": keep what works, throw out what doesn't. The genuinely open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying "this road didn't work, let's try another" — without that tolerance, experimentation won't get far.

points.h: The more flexible, the less anyone takes you seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that is depleted by capriciousness — credibility. Farrell cites Nobel economics laureate Thomas Schelling's argument: one of a nation's most important assets is credibility; commitments and threats that can be cashed are what actually work in negotiation. If you change your mind at any moment, and a threat you swore by the day before yesterday vanishes the next day, then at a certain point no one takes you seriously anymore. Farrell thinks America is in that state today: other countries still fear its capacity to do harm, but no longer believe it has the capacity for long-term action. His image: a drunken grandfather holding a shotgun, and everyone just humors him so he won't fire.

points.h: America is smashing its own web with a sledgehammer
points.body: The core question in Farrell and Newman's Underground Empire is this: globalization is a web of interdependence — supply chains interlock across dozens of countries and thousands of suppliers, and dollar clearing is the web's nerve center. America built this system with one hand and kept a "house advantage" with the other, using the threat of cutting off network access to constrain others. What the Trump administration is doing now is not delicately dismantling the web but swinging a sledgehammer at its parts semi-randomly. Farrell's direction from this is clear: complete decoupling from one another would be a disaster, and what countries can do is not become independent but give interdependence resilience, while getting the major powers to relearn how to talk about "restraint."

points.h: One rare-earth card punctures the invincibility thesis
points.body: On last year's "tariff big day," Bessent said publicly that America was holding all aces and China had no cards at all. Weeks later China played the rare-earth and critical-minerals card, and America suddenly realized it was holding a busted flush — cards that looked fierce but had never come together. Farrell sees this as the key moment that sobered Washington, and since then you can see that recognition in speeches by Marco Rubio and others: China has the capacity to materially hurt the US economy. The US and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows "I can badly hurt you," but they have not yet truly sat down to negotiate that balance into more stable rules.

terms.def: God's existence cannot be proven, but believing in Him has a higher expected payoff; Bessent swaps this for "obeying America is safer."

A concept Farrell relays from Abe Newman and Stacey Goddard: the world economy carved up by family and patronage networks rather than national interest.
A poker term: one card short of a flush; America discovers its hand is actually a pile of junk.
